justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 455 was anchored heavily on the most recent observed value and short-term momentum, assuming no major discontinuities in whatever underlying series this represents. The one-week estimate of 458 incorporates a slight upward trend extrapolation, reflecting the assumption that whatever directional pressure was present in recent data would persist at a modest pace. The one-month estimate of 463 extends that logic further, though the incremental change from the one-week figure is intentionally small, acknowledging that mean-reverting forces often dampen longer-run drift.

Confidence interval widths widen as expected across horizons, reflecting the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 17 units, consistent with the assumption that short-term variance in this series is bounded and that no major scheduled events were imminent. By one week, the interval expands to plus or minus 30 units, incorporating uncertainty around how external conditions might evolve over several trading or calendar days. At one month, the interval widens to plus or minus 58 units, reflecting the much broader range of macroeconomic, policy, or structural developments that could shift the series meaningfully over a four-week period.

There are several risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as a policy announcement, better-than-expected data release, or a shift in market sentiment could push the series well above 521 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a sudden shock — whether a geopolitical event, financial market dislocation, or negative data surprise — could easily breach the lower bound of 405. These tail risks are real but were assessed as low-probability relative to the central scenario.

It is also worth noting that the intervals assume a reasonably stationary volatility regime. If volatility were to spike — as it can during periods of stress — the actual distribution of outcomes would be fat-tailed, meaning the stated 90% confidence intervals might understate true uncertainty. Any structural break in the underlying data-generating process, such as a regime change in policy or market structure, would similarly render these forecasts poorly calibrated.
